title: 37 Integrating camera and microphone monitoring to evaluate immune responses and behavioral indicators in beef cattle using lipopolysaccharide administration as a model
content:
Abstract
This study investigated immune responses and behavioral alterations in Angus steers subjected to an intravenous (i.v.) lipopolysaccharide (LPS) challenge, utilizing an integrated camera and microphone monitoring system for comprehensive assessment. Twelve Angus steers were housed in four feedlot pens (3 steers/pen) with free-choice access to a corn-silage-based diet, water, and a commercial mineral-vitamin mix. Steers were weighed daily from days −3 to −1 of the experiment, and values were averaged to determine the initial BW (400 ± 6,0 kg). On day 0 (0700 h), steers were ranked by initial BW, divided into 2 groups in a crossover design, and assigned to one of two treatments at hour 0: 1) an i.v. bolus dose of bacterial LPS (0.5 μg/kg of BW; Escherichia coli 0111; Sigma-Aldrich Corp., St. Louis, MO), or 2) a 5 mL i.v. injection of 0.9% sterile saline (CON). Bacterial LPS was dissolved in 5 mL of 0.9% saline immediately before administration and was infused using a 10 mL sterile syringe according to the initial steer BW. The experimental period lasted 9 days (days −3 to 6) with 10 days of washout between periods. Samples of offers and refusals were collected to calculate the dry matter intake (DMI) after the challenge. Rectal temperatures were monitored using a GLA M750 digital thermometer at 0 (before administration), 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post administration. The monitoring system comprised security cameras mounted 15 feet high and positioned 5 feet from pens, providing comprehensive coverage, while coin-sized microphones attached to custom 3D-printed halters captured breathing patterns. The images captured by the cameras were processed using YOLOv11 to detect the positions of steers within the pen. A perspective transformation was then applied to correct distortion from the camera angle, enabling the creation of a heatmap indicating steer locations in the pen. Microphone data was processed with the Librosa library to visualize breathing patterns as Mel spectrograms. The AI-based monitoring system demonstrated early detection capabilities, identifying behavioral changes within the first 3 hours following LPS administration before traditional clinical signs emerged. LPS-challenged steers exhibited distinctive respiratory patterns, characterized by sharper and deeper breaths, and showed altered spatial behavior, congregating at the back of pens and avoiding feed areas (Fig.1). The rectal temperature increased (P < 0.01) markedly at 4 hours post-LPS administration. This elevation persisted for 12 hours before normalizing. Feed intake suppression in LPS-challenged steers extended (P < 0.01) for 72 hours post-administration. The integration of AI-based monitoring with cameras and microphones demonstrated significant potential for detecting early immune responses and behavioral indicators, offering a valuable tool for identifying early signs of diseases in beef cattle production systems.
